content: Gutka, also spelled as gutkha, guttkha, or guthka, is a preparation made from crushed betel nut, tobacco, and various sweet or savory flavorings. It is primarily manufactured in India and exported to a limited number of other countries. This product acts as a mild stimulant and is widely sold across India in small, individual-sized packets, typically priced between 1 and 4 rupees each. Gutka is consumed in a manner similar to chewing tobacco. However, like chewing tobacco, it is strongly associated with the development of oral cancer and other severe adverse health effects. Despite its harmful nature, gutka is used by millions of adults and is also marketed to children. Some packaging does not disclose tobacco as an ingredient, and certain brands are presented as candies, featuring brightly colored packaging and images of children. Some variants are chocolate-flavored, while others are marketed as breath fresheners. The substance itself is a powdery, granular white material that is placed between the lower lip and gum or under the tongue. Within moments of placement, gutka begins to dissolve and turns a deep red color. It produces a buzz that is reportedly more intense than that of tobacco. Gutka is highly addictive and is classified as a known carcinogen. Its widespread use has sparked significant controversy in India. Many states have attempted to curb its popularity by imposing heavy taxes on its sale or outright banning it. Gutka use often begins at a very young age. Its sweet taste, affordability, and easy availability make it particularly appealing to poor children, who may develop precancerous lesions at an early age as a result of its consumption. Some children perceive gutka as a type of candy. Symptoms of cancer frequently manifest by the time these individuals reach high school or college age. Social norms in India generally discourage children from smoking cigarettes, but gutka use, being discreet and less noticeable, has become a preferred alternative. After consumption, users typically spit the remnants onto walls or the ground, leaving unsightly red stains that are resistant to weathering. In response to this issue, some building owners have painted murals of deities on their walls, hoping that gutka users would refrain from spitting on images of gods. On August 1, 2002, the state of Maharashtra implemented a five-year ban on all gutka use, classifying it as a potentially hazardous food product. However, an active black market for gutka persisted during this period. Eventually, the High Court of Judicature at Mumbai overturned the ban, citing concerns over unfair trade practices.
